summary: Advises network operators who have an OSI NSAP addressing plan and want to move to IPv6 to design a fresh native IPv6 plan rather than reuse the old one. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 4048.

eli5.summary: If you are moving to a new house, do not try to reuse the old floor plan. Draw a new one that fits the new place. This note told people to do exactly that with their network addresses.

subtitle: How to carry OSI NSAP addresses in IPv6 networks, and why the authors say to redesign your addressing plan instead.

tldr.problem: Some networks had planned or deployed OSI NSAP addresses (up to 20 bytes) and wanted to move to IPv6, whose addresses are 16 bytes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends redesigning a native IPv6 addressing plan, but defines four elective mechanisms for those who still need NSAPs: a restricted mapping, a truncated NSAP, a destination option carrying the full NSAP, and an IPv6 address embedded inside an NSAP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1888 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 4048 and updated by RFC 4548.

today: RFC 1888 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 4048 and updated by RFC 4548.

sections.title: Redesign, Do Not Reuse
sections.content:
This experimental memo is aimed at implementors who already planned or deployed an OSI NSAP addressing plan for CLNP and now want to deploy or transition to IPv6. Its general recommendation is that they SHOULD design a native IPv6 addressing plan according to RFC 1884, as a natural re-mapping of the CLNP plan.

An NSAP address (NSAPA) can be up to 20 bytes long, while an IPv6 address is 16 bytes. Most known CLNP plans use the DCC or ICD formats, and these can normally be split into a high-order part for the network service provider and a low-order part for the user network and hosts.

The RFC uses US GOSIP as an example. There the high-order part is 9 bytes and the low-order part (Area and ID) is 8 bytes. The high-order part would be replaced by a provider prefix, with an 8-byte prefix recommended, and the low-order part mapped into the low-order half of the IPv6 address. The 6-byte ID field can serve as the token for IPv6 autoconfiguration.
sections.eli5: The best advice is to draw a fresh address map for the new network, keeping the useful parts of the old one, instead of cramming the old map into the new space.

sections.title: Three Warnings About the Mismatch
sections.content:
The RFC lists three warnings to weigh in every case when mapping a CLNP plan into IPv6.

  • Areas versus subnets. ES-IS and IS-IS route down to the Area, and end systems in one Area need not share a link. IPv6 routing goes down to the subnet, and all hosts in a subnet are assumed to be on one link. An extra level of hierarchy may be needed, so an Area number cannot blindly be used as a subnet number.
  • Aggregation. Subnet addresses should aggregate to keep routing tables small, so all subnets should share the same prefix whether they use pure IPv6 or a CLNP-derived scheme.
  • Multiple interfaces. An OSI end system may have several NSAPs that each identify the host as a whole. In IPv6 each physical interface must have its own unique addresses.

The document does not cover migrating the ES-IS or IS-IS routing protocols or the network infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The old system and the new one count "neighborhoods" differently, so you cannot just copy the old street numbers across. You may need to add an extra level, such as a block number.

sections.title: The Four Mechanisms
sections.content:
For those who need NSAPs anyway, the RFC defines four ELECTIVE mechanisms. They are not mandatory parts of IPv6, but if used they MUST be implemented as defined here.

  1. Restricted NSAPA mapping into a 16-byte IPv6 address.
  2. Truncated NSAPA for routing, with the full NSAPA in an IPv6 option.
  3. Normal IPv6 address, with the full NSAPA in an IPv6 option.
  4. IPv6 address carried as an OSI address.

The first byte of the IPv6 address tells them apart. If it is hexadecimal 0x02, the remaining 15 bytes hold a restricted NSAPA. If it is 0x03, they hold a truncated NSAPA, and then either a destination option with the complete NSAPA or an encapsulated CLNP packet must be present. With any other address, a destination option with a full NSAPA may be present.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to tuck an old-style address into the new system, like four different envelopes. The first byte of the new address tells you which envelope you are holding.

sections.title: Restricted and Truncated NSAPAs
sections.content:
A restricted NSAPA maps a subset of the ICD and DCC formats into the 16 bytes after the 0x02 byte. The mapping is algorithmic and reversible within that subset. A 4-bit AFcode says which format is used: values 0 to 9 imply AFI 47 (ICD) and are the first digit of the ICD, 1010 implies AFI 39 (DCC), and the rest are reserved. The NSEL octet is not included. The RFC warns that choosing this route has serious routing implications, because routing between such organizations and the rest of the Internet is unlikely to be optimised.

Restricted NSAPAs can be routed hierarchically down to the Area but must be flat-routed within it. If an Area spans more than one subnet and router, no IPv6 routing protocol can route to the final router, and the RFC offers no solution within existing IPv6 mechanisms. Restricted NSAPAs also do not aggregate with normal IPv6 addresses.

A truncated NSAPA follows the 0x03 byte with the high-order octets of the NSAP, cut off and zero padded if needed. It may be treated as an anycast address when used as a destination, for example to identify the endpoint of a CLNP tunnel. Used as a source, it must be unique unicast. Either an NSAPA destination option or an encapsulated CLNP packet MUST be present. Routing it is called a grey area: if possible, a GOSIP-like NSAPA should be truncated just after the Area number.
sections.eli5: One way squeezes the old address into the new slot exactly, which works only for some kinds. The other way writes just the front part of the old address and tapes the full one to the side.

sections.title: The NSAPA Destination Option
sections.content:
When a truncated NSAPA is used other than for a CLNP tunnel, the full NSAPA travels in an IPv6 destination option. The option type code is 11-0-00011, which is 195 decimal. It carries an option data length, a source NSAP length and a destination NSAP length (each one octet), followed by the source and destination NSAPs. With standard 20-octet NSAPs the total option length is 44 bytes and the option data length is 42.

The destination node should check that Option Data Length equals Source NSAP Length plus Dest. NSAP Length plus 2. On inconsistency it discards the packet and sends an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 2, pointing at the Option Data Length field. IPv6 nodes need not implement the option, except nodes using truncated NSAPAs other than for CLNP tunnels.

Annex B explains that a destination option was chosen over a new extension header so that intermediate nodes can ignore it without understanding its syntax. Only nodes that care about NSAPs need to know about it.
sections.eli5: It is a label stuck on the packet holding the full old address. Nodes in the middle can ignore the label, and only the ones that care read it.

sections.title: IPv6 Inside an NSAP, and Security
sections.content:
The reverse direction is also defined. If an IPv6 address must be embedded in a 20-octet NSAP, a fixed format MUST be used. The first three octets are an IDP in binary format: AFI value 35 (provisionally allocated, pending a change to ISO 8348) and an Internet Code Point of zero. The 16 IPv6 bytes follow, and the last octet is a selector with a default of zero and no significance for IPv6. Conversion back strips the first three and the twentieth octets.

To avoid routing anomalies or loops, an embedded IPv6 address MUST NOT have the prefixes 0x02 or 0x03, and an NSAPA with the IANA AFI code MUST NOT be embedded in an IPv6 header. The memo suggests uses such as expressing an IP address in the ATM Forum address format.

On security, the RFC says only that the mechanisms are compatible with the IPv6 security mechanisms of RFC 1825 and that security is not specifically addressed.
sections.eli5: You can also go the other way and put a new-style address inside an old-style envelope, as long as you never nest the envelopes inside each other.
